title: Hymns
author: Plethon
translator: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), from the Greek of the Alexandre edition of 1858

lines.text: Hymns

Plethon's twenty-seven hymns to the gods, from chapter 35 of Book III of his Book of Laws, in the Greek text of C. Alexandre's edition (Paris, 1858, pp. 202–228). They are the perennial, monthly, sacred and daily hymns of his restored Hellenic worship, addressed to Zeus, to Poseidon and Hera, to the Olympians, to the Titans and daemons, and closing with daily prayers and beatitudes on the virtuous life. This translation is made directly from the Greek, line for line, nine lines to each hymn. Public domain.
I — Perennial Hymn to Zeus

Father Zeus, father of yourself, eldest creator, king and begetter of all, most high, surpassing all, all-powerful, being itself, the One itself, and the Good itself; you who from boundless eternity begot all these things, the greater by yourself, and the rest through them, each of such a kind and in such measure as was best: be gracious and save us, leading us too, with the whole of things, through your ever-glorious children, to whom you gave the charge, in the way that our lot also is ordained by you, to the end that was due.
II — Perennial Hymn to the Gods

Glorious children and lieutenants of Zeus, who is being itself and begetter of all, you who guide us with justice: may we never cease to have you as our leaders, nor to follow the right laws, the laws dear to you, as far as we are able, which alone order us well. But you, O gods, who steer the charioteer intellect within us, which you settled in us as kin to yourselves, grant that in all else too we may lead our life well, and grant that with you we may hymn Zeus last of all.
III — First Monthly Hymn to Zeus

Great Zeus, truly Janus, father of himself and forefather of all things to which being and becoming belong, has made none of them on a sudden; but for as long as he himself has been, for so long has he been making these too in like manner, never idle, nor ever doing good in less than his own full power, as indeed he must, being the very thing that is Good. Hail, O Zeus, ruler of all, most kingly! Hail, O supremely blessed! Hail, unstinting giver of good things!
IV — Second Monthly Hymn to Poseidon

O great lord Poseidon, firstborn son of Zeus, who surpass in splendour and in strength the whole of this generation, all that comes from Zeus, over which, second after your father, you received mighty rule and kingship, while he in turn surpasses all things beyond all measure, since he alone of all that is is wholly ungenerated. To you it fell, at your father's bidding, to fashion this wide heaven too, in which we also have been born to you; to us, then, be always gentle and gracious, O father.
V — Third Monthly Hymn to Hera

Hera, august goddess, daughter of great Zeus, whose husband is Poseidon, he who is the very thing that is Beautiful; mother of the gods within the heaven, bringer-forth of matter, the seat of the forms here below, and giver of every power, of every other kind and of that which leads to virtue and to all splendour; you who gather the laws from which, for the whole of things, multitude and eternity alike have come to be: to us also grant to live well, graciously leading us on to virtue.
VI — Fourth Monthly Hymn to the Olympian Gods

Lord Poseidon, best child of great Zeus, who hold from your father the leadership of this whole generation; and you, Hera, his pure wife and noble queen; Apollo and Artemis, Hephaestus and Bacchus, and Athena: you seven gods who are mightier than all the rest, after the surpassing ruler on high; and you others who dwell on Olympus, who are fathers of the immortals here below, and of us among them: be gracious to us and kindly.
VII — Fifth Monthly Hymn to Apollo

Lord Apollo, who over the nature of the Same in each thing stand as guardian and leader; you who bring things, one with another, into one, and set the All itself, many-parted though it is and many-stringed, beneath a single harmony: from concord you bestow on souls wisdom and justice, the fairest of good things, and on bodies health, and beauty as well; give always, then, a longing for divine beauties, O lord, to our souls. Hail, Paean!
VIII — Sixth Monthly Hymn to Artemis

Lady Artemis, you who lead the nature of the Other and preside over it: for you receive the All as one and then divide it, this way and that, to the very last, into many forms, and from the forms into individuals, and from wholes again into parts and limbs; and to souls, by their separation from what is worse, you give courage and temperance, and to bodies in turn strength and soundness. But, O lady, grant us at every turn escape from what is shameful, and set upright our life with its many falls.
IX — Seventh Monthly Hymn to the Heavenly Gods

O Helios, lord of this heaven, be gracious; be gracious too, Selene, holy lady; and you, Phosphorus and Stilbon, the two bright attendants ever at the side of Helios; and you, Phaenon, Phaethon and Pyroeis, who all are lieutenants of the lord Helios, and in the providence that is over us work with him wherever there is need: we too hymn you, our glorious guardians, and with you the other stars, sent forth by divine foreknowledge.
X — Eighth Monthly Hymn to Athena

Lady Athena, you who guard and lead the form that is nowhere separable from matter, being yourself its creator, after the wide-ruling Poseidon, who holds all form prior to you; you who are the cause of all motion that arises by thrust, and whatever superfluous thing accrues you yourself drive out from each; from us too, whenever in our folly something discordant draws near, drive it away, O goddess, rousing our spirit with intellect to what is needful.
XI — Ninth Monthly Hymn to Dionysus

Father Bacchus, begetter of all rational souls, the heavenly, and the daemonic, and our own, after lord Poseidon; you who are the cause of the motion drawn by love of the good and of the ascent toward what is better: grant us too, whenever through foolish judgment we fall away from good and more godly action, to be led swiftly back to it again with intellect, and do not leave us long in folly about the things that are good.
XII — Tenth Monthly Hymn to the Titans

Come, let us hymn the creator of the whole of mortal nature, lord Cronus, son of Zeus, eldest of all the other, illegitimate children of Zeus, the Titans of Tartarus; and them too, along with him, let us hymn, all of them noble and untouched by doom, though they beget things mortal and subject to doom: Aphrodite, the holy wife of this same Cronus, Pan, ruler of beasts, and Demeter, of plants, and Kore, of our mortal part, and all the rest.
XIII — Eleventh Monthly Hymn to Hephaestus

Lord Hephaestus, you who lead the gods beyond the heaven, Olympian and Tartarean alike, and preside over them, after the wide-ruling Poseidon, and allot to each of them a place and a seat; you who are the cause of rest in the Same, for the whole and for each thing, to which you furnish eternity, you yourself, or Poseidon, by the counsels of his father: guard us also, and grant us, whenever we are engaged in noble actions, to abide in them a very long while.
XIV — Twelfth Monthly Hymn to the Daemons

With the other immortals let us hymn also those nearest to us, these pure daemons, who serve the other, more divine gods right well in what concerns us, and give us many things, all of them noble, which all come to them from Zeus himself, descending through the other gods; and so they keep us safe, some by purifying us, some by leading us upward, others by guarding us, with great ease setting our intellect upright. Be gracious, then.
XV — Thirteenth Monthly Hymn to All the Gods

Zeus most high, who surpass all the gods, being the eldest creator and begetter of all; and you, all you gods, Olympian and Tartarean, heavenly and earthly: if there is in us some grievous fault, or reckless deeds, grant that, cleansed of them, we may draw near to you, the blameless, so that our life too may become blessed; and you, O Zeus, above all, who are most sovereign over all, being yourself at once the very first good and the last.
XVI — First Sacred Hymn to Zeus

Zeus alone is wholly ungenerated and being itself, begetter of all and ruler of all; he holds all things hidden in himself as one, with nothing apart, and from himself sends each forth distinctly, and so completes his work as again one single whole, wholly full and most beautiful so far as was possible, for he is one and wholly without envy. But, O Zeus, lead us too, through your glorious children, together with the whole, steering us as you have determined; and grant us to begin our undertakings well, and to bring our deeds to completion.
XVII — Second Sacred Hymn to the Olympian Gods

Come, let us hymn lord Poseidon, who is the eldest of all the children of Zeus and the mightiest, ruler, second after his father, of this whole generation, and our immediate creator; and with him queen Hera, who in turn was born to father Zeus the eldest of goddesses; and let us hymn the others too, all the gods on Olympus, who are all guardians and co-causes of the immortals here below. Be gracious to us, then.
XVIII — Third Sacred Hymn to All the Gods

O all you gods who, after Zeus the supremely good, are yourselves wholly blameless and untouched by doom; of whom Poseidon is chief, and ruler from Zeus; you who are beyond the heaven and you within the heaven, all of you glorious: you we hymn, we who also have a nature akin to yours, though we are the last. Hail, you who are yourselves blessed, and givers of good things! And to us, whose life is not always free of care, allot in turn what is fine and noble, and raise us upright always.
XIX — Fourth Sacred Hymn to All the Gods after the Olympians

O lord Cronus, who rule even over the Titans beyond the heaven; and you who in turn lead this heaven, Helios, the whole of it, whom the other planets follow: from you two the whole generation of mortals has sprung, from the pair of you, Cronus and Helios; and the Titans and the planets, your lieutenants, work with you, each in a different task. You too we hymn, since through you also we have many noble things; and with you the fixed stars, and the pure daemons.
XX — Fifth Sacred Hymn to Pluto

O lord Pluto, ruler and guardian of human nature, a charge allotted you by Zeus himself; holding as one all that comes to be in us and dwells in us separately, govern us well, both wholly here below, and ever leading us up again from here; around you are the heroes, the nature that surpasses ours, and our other friends, the fine and good; and with you dwells Kore, the noble goddess of Tartarus, who binds the mortal part to us as long as is needful. Be gracious.
XXI — Sixth Sacred Hymn to Zeus

Father Zeus, mighty in works, great in strength, sovereign of good things, begetter of all: by your intellect, since you are supremely good, not even we were born without a share in the fine things that are in the gods; yet by the necessity of our mortal part we are at once prone to err and always able to be set right again. Grant us, then, now too, released from the evil of our errors through your children, to whom you gave this charge, to draw near to the pure, who keep an upright intellect, so that we may ever commune with you, who are gentle and gracious.
XXII — First Daily Hymn (Second Day)

May I never cease, O blessed gods, to be grateful to you for the good things that all come to me through you, and always have, whose highest giver is Zeus. May I never neglect the common good of my own kind, so far as lies in my power; but gladly serving the common good, may I know it to be at once my own great gain. May I never be the cause of harm to any man I may meet, but of good, as far as I am able, so that, made like to you, I too may become blessed.
XXIII — Second Daily Hymn (Third Day)

May there be no disorder in me, O gods, in sweet pleasures, but may I accept a limit to them, such that no ill comes from them to soul or to body. May I never be insatiable for wealth; but may I set a measure to this also, by the body's orderly need, so that I may rejoice in self-sufficiency. May I never be overcome by empty, beguiling glory, knowing that the only good in it is whatever leads to divine and true virtue.
XXIV — Third Daily Hymn (Fourth Day)

May fortunes never cast me down, O gods, whenever they strike down my mortal part, for I know that my soul is immortal, separable from the mortal, and divine. May none of the harsh things that come from men trouble me at all, as I train myself in freedom and am not, through some base notion, a slave to those who are worse. May I never, when it falls to me to act for the sake of the noble, spare my mortal part; but may it always be my care that my soul, being immortal, should be at its best.
XXV — Fourth Daily Hymn (Fifth Day)

Blessed is he who cares always for his immortal soul, that it may become as fair as possible, and for his mortal part has no great concern, and at need does not spare it. Blessed is he who never makes himself a slave to mortals who senselessly strike at him, but, keeping his soul unshaken, rises above their wickedness. Blessed is he who, when the fortunes sent by the daemons turn bitter, does not grieve in soul, but bears them lightly, placing the good in his own immortal part alone.
XXVI — Fifth Daily Hymn (Sixth Day)

Blessed is he who pays no foolish heed to the empty opinions of mortals, but, heeding himself in his own right thinking, practises divine virtue with upright judgment. Blessed is he who does not forever chase a boundless heap of possessions, rashly and at random, but by the fitting needs of the body sets the measure of them. Blessed is he who keeps a due bound to enjoyment, one that draws no ill upon his soul or upon his body, but is in harmony with divine virtue.
XXVII — Sixth Daily Hymn (Seventh Day)

Blessed is he who does not grasp at private gain and, through dreadful folly, work evils for men, but always good, like the blessed gods themselves. Blessed is he who does not neglect the common good of his own kind, but, knowing that the gods too care for the common good, never himself betrays it. Blessed is he who is grateful to the gods for whatever good things are his, and above all to Zeus himself, from whom, as first source, all that is fine and noble comes forth to all.
